noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Cost
title: Ideas are cheap. Shipping is expensive.
quote: It turned out that the materials cost of a rocket was around 2% of the typical price. 98 cents of every dollar was going somewhere other than what it was made of — supplier markup stacking through contract layers, custom designs that couldn't achieve manufacturing scale, and expendable hardware thrown away after every flight.
bridgeText: In product, the equivalent of 'atoms' is ideas. They're essentially free. The expensive part is engineering time, coordination, context-switching, and review cycles. A PM who generates 100 ideas but can't ruthlessly prioritize is doing exactly what traditional aerospace did: adding cost at every layer with no accountability for where the dollars are going. Ask yourself: what percentage of your team's time is going to actual product vs. process overhead?
actionText: Run an 'idiot index' on your roadmap. For every feature, ask: what's the ratio of eng weeks spent to actual user value delivered? High ratio = you're being an idiot (Elon's words, not mine). The most over-engineered features in any backlog are usually the ones nobody questioned because a smart stakeholder asked for them.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Requirements
title: The best feature is no feature.
quote: The best part is no part. The best process is no process.
bridgeText: PMs inherit requirements from executives, customers, legal, and 'how we've always done it.' SpaceX's rule: every requirement must have an owner who can defend why it still exists. If the owner can't explain it, or the original reason no longer applies, delete it. The requirements from 'smart people' are the most dangerous: nobody thinks to question them.
actionText: At your next sprint planning, pick one requirement that's been on the list for months and ask: who owns this? Can they defend it in 60 seconds? If not, put it in a 'delete pending' column for two weeks and see if anyone notices it's missing.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Validation
title: Ship to learn. Not to be right.
quote: You can't think your way to perfect solutions for problems you don't fully understand. Your model is always wrong in the ways you don't know yet. Complex systems have emergent behaviors that only appear when the pieces are actually bolted together. The alternative is to use reality as your primary validation tool.
bridgeText: The PM equivalent of Boeing's 'analyze before building' is endless PRD writing, stakeholder alignment rounds, and design reviews before a single line of code ships. Every week you spend perfecting a spec is a week you're not finding out where your model is wrong. SpaceX literally publishes its failures. 'How Not to Land an Orbital Rocket,' a compilation video of rockets exploding, set to music. What's your version of that?
actionText: For your next feature, identify the single riskiest assumption: the one that, if wrong, makes the whole thing pointless. Now ask: what's the smallest thing you could ship in two weeks that would tell you whether that assumption is true or false? That's your Starship prototype.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Cadence
title: Shipping cadence is a superpower.
quote: A high production rate solves many ills. Any given technology development is how many iterations do you have, and what's your time and progress between iterations? So if you have a high production rate, you can have a lot of iterations. You can try a lot of different things.
bridgeText: A PM who ships weekly has 52 data points a year. A PM who ships quarterly has 4. Shipping cadence is a learning rate multiplier. The teams that look magically effective after 2 years aren't smarter. They've had more iterations. SpaceX didn't nail booster landings because they were geniuses. They had 20 attempts at the same problem. Most product teams get 3.
actionText: Count how many times your team shipped something users could actually interact with in the last 90 days. Now count the number of planning meetings. If the ratio is off, you have a cadence problem, not a quality problem. Ship smaller things more often. Even a one-line copy change is a feedback loop.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Focus
title: What's your Raptor engine?
quote: When Starship development was bottlenecked on Raptor Engine production, that became the company's focus. Not propellant loading, not heat shields, not launch infrastructure — Raptors. Elon gave it absolute focus, daily updates, memos to the company, resources redirected from elsewhere. Once engine production broke through, attention shifted to the next constraint. The limiter always gets the hammer.
bridgeText: PMs are famously bad at this. Spreading a team across 10 initiatives simultaneously is the norm. That's how you get 10 things at 40% instead of 2 things at 100%. At any given moment there is one constraint that, if removed, unlocks everything downstream. Your job is to identify it, name it out loud, and put disproportionate resources on it until it's gone. Then find the next one.
actionText: Ask your team: if we could only make one thing faster or better this quarter, what would it be? The answer is your Raptor engine. Write it down. Put it at the top of every planning doc. Check every other initiative against it: does this help the Raptor problem? If not, it moves to the back of the queue.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Vision
title: Clear mission makes prioritization automatic.
quote: Building cities on other planets isn't just aspirational branding. It's a sorting mechanism. The mission attracts missionaries.
bridgeText: A product vision is a decision-making tool, not decor. When your vision is sharp enough, 80% of prioritization debates resolve themselves because the answer is obvious against the stated goal. If your team argues about priority in every planning meeting, that's usually a signal the vision is too vague to be useful. The vision is also a recruiting filter: people who believe in it will work harder than people who just think it's a reasonable job.
actionText: Write your product vision in one sentence. Now test it: take two features from your backlog that you're currently debating and apply the vision as a filter. Does one clearly win? If you still can't tell, the vision isn't sharp enough yet. Keep refining until it gives you answers, not more questions.

noteTitle: 7 lessons SpaceX taught me about product
label: On Systems
title: Structure beats heroics. Every time.
quote: The answer to what's hard to copy isn't any single tactic. It's that the tactics are a system. Copy one without the others and it breaks down. The lesson isn't 'be like Elon.' Hero worship is the wrong takeaway. One person didn't build Starship. The lesson is that structure matters more than the hero. Get the system right, and the results follow.
bridgeText: The best product teams aren't the ones with the most brilliant PM. They're the ones with the best feedback loops, the clearest constraints, and the cultural tolerance for visible failure. Your job as a PM is to build the system that makes great outcomes repeatable. Not to be the hero who personally solves every hard problem. If your team falls apart when you're out sick for a week, that's a system problem, not a vacation problem.
actionText: How fast are your feedback loops? How fast can you get to reality? The moment your team starts resolving issues two cycles after you identify them, the drag coefficient has arrived.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Performance
title: Before you coach the person, fix the system.
quote: The biggest changes weren't the model or the prompts. They were: how the task was broken down, how state was tracked, how key steps were validated, and how failures were recovered from. Same model, same prompts — success rate went from under 70% to above 95%.
bridgeText: When someone on your team keeps underdelivering, the instinct is to coach harder, give more feedback, or eventually replace them. This is the same mistake as blaming the model. The fix in this story wasn't the person — it was task decomposition, handoff clarity, checkpoints, and recovery paths. Before your next performance conversation, ask: have I designed the system this person is operating in, or am I just hoping they figure it out?
actionText: Pick one underperforming team member. Before your next 1:1, map the work they're doing: how the task gets handed to them, what information they have, when they're supposed to check in, and what happens when something goes wrong. Fix one structural gap before adjusting the coaching conversation.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Leadership
title: Your job is designing the environment, not assigning the tasks.
quote: Humans don't need to write a single line of code. Humans need to design the environment. When something fails, don't ask it to try harder — ask what capability is missing from the environment.
bridgeText: This is the most direct management lesson in the podcast. The environment you design includes: how work is scoped, what context people have, what the feedback loop looks like, what the rules of escalation are, and what 'good' is defined as. That's your job. The team is capable. The harness — your management system — is what's missing. When your team fails, your first question shouldn't be 'why didn't they work harder?' — it should be 'what did I fail to put in place?'
actionText: After your next project post-mortem, replace the question 'what did the team do wrong?' with 'what was missing from the environment?' Run through: did they have the right task definition? The right information at the right time? A clear success criterion? A way to recover when things went sideways? Fix the environment before fixing the people.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Communication
title: More information doesn't mean better work.
quote: Optimizing context isn't about giving more — it's about giving on-demand, in layers, at the right moment.
bridgeText: Most managers over-brief. Long kickoff documents, packed strategy decks, 'here's everything you need to know' emails. The research here suggests this actively hurts performance — more information at once means less useful attention on any of it. The better model: share the core goal upfront, provide reference material only when the person is at the decision point where it's relevant. Just-in-time context beats just-in-case context.
actionText: Look at the last project brief you sent. Count the number of things in it that the team won't need until week 3. Move those to a follow-up or a linked doc. Write briefs with one goal, the immediate decision needed, and a pointer to deeper context if required. See if the questions you get back become more focused.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Quality
title: Self-review is structurally optimistic.
quote: Separate the person doing the work from the person validating it. The evaluator doesn't just review code — it actually operates the UI, checks real interactions, verifies actual results. Production and acceptance must be separated. As long as the evaluator is sufficiently independent, the system forms a genuinely effective loop.
bridgeText: If you only ask people to self-assess their work, you'll consistently get optimistic results — especially on qualitative, hard-to-measure work. This isn't a character flaw; it's structural. Anthropic's solution was architectural: a completely separate Evaluator that actually runs the output in the real environment. For a manager, your review mechanisms need independence built in — peer review, external stakeholders, defined rubrics someone other than the author applies.
actionText: For your team's next major deliverable, define the acceptance criteria before the work starts — and assign someone other than the author to verify them. Even a lightweight rubric evaluated by a teammate beats the author's own confidence rating every time.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Resilience
title: Design for failure before it designs you.
quote: In real environments, failure is the norm, not the exception. Without recovery mechanisms, every agent error means starting from scratch. A mature harness always includes three things: constraints (what can and can't be done), checkpoints (how to verify before and after), and recovery (how to restart, reroute, or roll back to a stable state).
bridgeText: Teams that treat every missed deadline or dropped ball as a crisis burn out fast and learn slowly. Teams that have designed for failure — clear escalation paths, blameless retros, defined rollback options, 'if X happens, do Y' protocols — treat the same events as normal operating conditions. The difference isn't team quality. It's whether the manager built a recovery harness or just hoped things wouldn't break.
actionText: Pick one recurring failure mode on your team (missed handoffs, unclear specs, late dependencies). Write a one-paragraph recovery protocol — not a blame assignment, but a defined response: who notices, who decides, what the fallback is. Share it with the team. Normalizing the failure scenario removes the panic and unlocks faster recovery.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Harness Engineering taught me about managing people
label: On Maturity
title: Management maturity has three layers. Most stop at one.
quote: Prompt engineering is engineering the instruction. Context engineering is engineering the input environment. Harness engineering is engineering the entire operating system. Each layer's boundary is larger than the last — and they're not substitutes. They stack.
bridgeText: Early-stage managers fix the instruction — clearer asks, better briefs. Mid-stage managers fix the context — making sure people have the right information, the right stakeholders, the right resources. Senior managers build the system — the norms, the rituals, the feedback loops, the failure protocols that run whether or not the manager is in the room. Most managers plateau at layer 1 or 2. The podcast is an argument for why layer 3 is where sustainable team performance actually lives.
actionText: If your best team member left tomorrow, how much of their performance would survive — because you built the system — versus disappear with them?

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Moats
title: The moat nobody could see from the outside
quote: It's always the data that you can't see that kills you. Because if you can see a truck coming at you, you're just going to dodge and get out the way. But if you can't see it, you're dead.
bridgeText: DoorDash's defensibility isn't the consumer app — it's the structured dataset built from years of operating in a chaotic physical world. There are 20 decomposable steps in a single delivery, each with its own failure modes: a homesick driver, a broken gate code, an item moved from aisle 6 to aisle 8 with no documentation. None of this exists in any scrapable dataset. It can only be learned by doing millions of orders. This is a classically underappreciated moat: operational complexity that looks replicable from the outside but requires years and billions of orders to actually build.
actionText: Ask for cohort-level on-time delivery improvement trends over time. That curve is the compounding value of physical world learning made visible — and the best proxy for whether the moat is real.

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Timing
title: The 1,000 days of divergence — the contrarian window
quote: The metrics on the inside — you see everything going the direction that you would hope as an entrepreneur. You see repeatability from city A to city B to city C. You see unit economics improving.
bridgeText: From 2016 to 2019, DoorDash operated in a state of maximum narrative-to-fundamentals divergence. External headlines: 'can't beat Uber, can't make money, toxic sector.' Internal reality: improving unit economics, expanding city repeatability, organic growth with zero marketing budget. The investors who passed were optimizing for narrative safety. The few who looked inside the metrics captured the majority of returns before the 2019 turnaround. The 1,000 days weren't a near-death story — they were an extended entry window that most investors let close without acting.
actionText: A company that survives 3 years of constrained capital with improving fundamentals has proven its unit economics are real, not manufactured by spend. Ask: what did retention, margin, and organic growth look like during the lean years, before the narrative recovered?

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Market Sizing
title: The TAM nobody calculated correctly
quote: There were about a million restaurants in the states, and maybe 20 to 25,000 of them offered deliveries. The real grand question was: what about everyone else?
bridgeText: The common investor mistake in 2013 was sizing the food delivery market as the existing delivery market — 25k restaurants, mostly pizza. DoorDash's actual TAM was enabling the other 975,000 restaurants to offer delivery for the first time. That's not a market share story; it's a market creation story. Investors who saw DoorDash as a GrubHub competitor were sizing a rounding error. The expansion into DashMart, fulfillment for Kroger and CVS, and autonomous delivery is all evidence that the real TAM was always 'everything inside a city' — and it's still expanding.
actionText: What percentage of current revenue comes from non-delivery services — advertising, data intelligence, fulfillment? What is the trajectory and margin profile of those lines vs. the core delivery take rate? This reveals how far the TAM expansion has actually progressed.

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Founder Quality
title: The CEO who still reads every customer complaint
quote: I still do customer support every day. I see them literally every single day. Those are freebies. How lucky am I to actually have a product in which people care enough to actually let me know something went wrong?
bridgeText: A public company CEO doing daily customer support at millions-of-orders scale is an extreme outlier. Tony personally debugs order logs and calls dashers after reading 2,000-word complaint emails. This isn't a ritual — it's how he catches the invisible data that dashboards miss. Companies led by founders who stay close to raw customer signal make fewer catastrophic product decisions. And when the CEO does it, the entire organization can't hide behind aggregate metrics — the cultural norm cascades downward.
actionText: Is this behavior institutionalized or bottlenecked on one person? Ask how customer support insights flow into the product roadmap and experimentation pipeline — and what happens to that signal if the founder steps back.

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Compounding
title: Experimentation culture as a compounding return
quote: If you can get the 5% out of tens of thousands of experiments to work in one year, that has the benefit on all your audience for the next year. And then you just keep going.
bridgeText: DoorDash runs hundreds of thousands of experiments per week. The 95% failure rate isn't a problem — it's the price of admission for the 5% that ship and permanently raise the baseline. Next year's experiments start from a higher floor. This is a compounding learning system, not a series of independent bets. This experimentation culture is extraordinarily hard to replicate quickly. It requires organizational discipline, the right instrumentation, a tolerance for failure, and enough order volume to generate statistically significant results.
actionText: What is the ratio of experiments run per engineer? What percentage reach statistical significance? These numbers reveal whether the experimentation culture is genuine infrastructure or an aspirational talking point in board decks.

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Capital Efficiency
title: Underfunded forces product discipline — and that's a feature
quote: If a company has no ability to compete with budget, you only have one way to compete: build a product that has better retention, better engagement. You have to.
bridgeText: Unable to buy growth for three years while Uber and Amazon outspent them, DoorDash was forced to earn every dollar of retention through product quality alone. This built genuine habits in both the team and the customer base — not habits manufactured by discounts or ads. Companies that grow on marketing spend often have hollow retention curves the moment spend stops. DoorDash's organic growth during 2016–2019 is evidence that their retention was real.
actionText: Pull retention curves stratified by acquisition channel — organic vs. paid. Organic cohorts should show structurally superior retention. If they don't, the product quality signal doesn't exist independently of the marketing budget.

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Revenue Expansion
title: The intelligence platform hiding inside a delivery company
quote: We're giving data back to them: when you're out of stock, when you're underpriced, when there's an opportunity to bundle SKUs that would grow your actual business. Why can't we do those things for you?
bridgeText: Every delivery generates data of extraordinary commercial value: real-time demand signals, pricing benchmarks across thousands of merchants, inventory accuracy, customer preference clustering. Merchants paying for intelligence that makes them more profitable is a fundamentally different revenue model than a delivery commission — higher margin, stickier, compounding. The delivery business is a trojan horse for becoming the operating system of local commerce.
actionText: What is the revenue per merchant relationship beyond delivery commissions? What is the upsell attach rate for advertising, intelligence, and fulfillment — and what does the curve look like over the first 24 months of a merchant relationship?

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Autonomous Infrastructure
title: The 'last 10 feet' as an investable infrastructure thesis
quote: It's very hard to drive a robotaxi into a crowded hub of merchants and actually somehow find parking and get access to the products by itself. We built DoorDash Dot, which can travel on the road but also on the sidewalk and in bike lanes — a much smaller form factor that solves the last 10 feet problem.
bridgeText: Competitors in autonomous mobility are optimizing for the highway problem. DoorDash is optimizing for the access problem — the final 10 feet of every delivery. The ability to navigate sidewalks, bike lanes, mall interiors, and crowded merchant hubs is an operational advantage that general-purpose robotaxis structurally cannot replicate. This is not a product feature — it's an infrastructure thesis. Six years from first internal project to road deployment in Arizona. That timeline is the moat: it cannot be shortcut by capital alone.
actionText: What is the staged CapEx roadmap for DoorDash Dot from pilot to national deployment? At what unit density does autonomous last-mile delivery become margin-accretive vs. human dasher delivery — and how far is the current deployment from that threshold?

noteTitle: 9 lessons DoorDash taught me about building in the physical world
label: On Network Effects
title: Community identity as a network effect — the softer moat
quote: The personality is given by who the businesses are. And therefore, you and your friends want to go frequent and hang out in those places. That's what makes a city feel awesome. And so I think that's an eternal mission worth fighting for.
bridgeText: Tony elevated DoorDash from a service provider to an economic utility — a guardian of local community identity. This emotional and civic mission creates a retention mechanism for merchants and consumers that pricing models alone can't quantify. Local economies instinctively favor platforms that visibly support local businesses. A platform embedded in the social fabric of neighborhoods is far more durable than one competing purely on take rates. It's also structurally difficult for a national incumbent like Amazon to replicate — local trust is earned neighborhood by neighborhood, not deployed from a distribution center.
actionText: Beyond NPS and revenue, what metrics track DoorDash's actual impact on local merchant survival rates? If the mission is measurable, the moat is defensible. If it's only a narrative, it isn't.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Architecture
title: One agent can't do it all.
quote: Where people stumble with OpenClaw is they think they can throw any task at a single agent and get great results. And then they get really frustrated. I don't think anybody has really unlocked a general-purpose agent that handles everything well. The reason is simple: context overload. It's the same thing we've seen in every LLM chat interface.
bridgeText: Claire runs nine agents, each scoped to one lane: Polly handles work, Finn handles family logistics, Sam does sales outreach, Howie preps podcast episodes. They don't cross streams. Her analogy is Slack channels — you wouldn't put all company communication in #general, so don't route all tasks to one agent. Context window is finite; specialized agents make better use of it. This is an architecture decision, not a technical one.
actionText: Map your agent tasks like you'd map Slack channels. What would you never post in #general? That's a separate agent. If you're building agent products: the question isn't 'how do we make one agent smarter' — it's 'what lanes of work should never share context?'

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Outcomes
title: Make the user look like a winner.
quote: The best way to success in B2B SaaS is getting somebody promoted and making them look good. I think about Howie — he just makes me look good every morning when I have a podcast episode to record. He sends me a reminder: 'Hey Claire, remember your meeting with Al. Just in case you forgot, here's who Al is. Here's all the stuff he's going to show.'
bridgeText: This is the right north star for any agent UX you're building. Not 'complete the task' — make the user feel like a winner after the interaction. Claire's agents don't just execute; they hype her up, flag the scheduling conflict before she misses it, draft the brief she didn't ask for. For any B2B PM building agent features: the moment isn't 'here's the output' — it's 'here's the output, and here's why you look sharp for knowing this.'
actionText: Rewrite your agent's success metric as: 'Did the user feel more capable after this interaction?' Audit your current agent outputs against that bar. If the output just completes the task but doesn't give the user a moment of 'I look good because of this,' there's a UX gap.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Management
title: Your management skills transfer directly.
quote: You don't need the technical skills. You need role scoping or design — how do we talk to customers, how do we talk to each other. The rest of it we can give to Claude Code to figure out.
bridgeText: Claire ran 20+ years of managing humans before managing agents — and she credits that, not engineering, for her success. The waterline model applies: if your agent keeps doing the wrong thing, it's a scoping or documentation failure, not a dumb AI. The same diagnostic applies to human teams. Define the job, give it the tools it needs, be explicit about what 'great' looks like. Then hold it to that bar.
actionText: Write your agent's job description like you'd write a JD for a human hire: title, responsibilities, what 'great' looks like, what's explicitly out of scope. Then check if your soul file or system prompt actually reflects that JD. Mismatch = root cause of most agent failures.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Trust
title: Earn access. Don't grant it.
quote: First you get my calendar, and then you can read my email, and then I guess you could draft some emails, and then you can send the emails. You don't onboard your EA by giving them the password to your email account. They have their own email, their own calendar, and you give them access or permission.
bridgeText: This isn't just a security posture — it's an onboarding design principle. Progressive permission flows aren't friction; they're trust scaffolding. For product builders: users who grant full agent access on day one are also the ones who abandon it after the first mistake. Design for graduated trust. Let the agent demonstrate competence at low-stakes tasks first. Expand scope after it's earned it.
actionText: Audit your agent's current permission level. What is it doing that you've never consciously approved? Design a 'trust level 2' that would be meaningfully more useful and requires demonstrated reliability at level 1 first. Map the permission expansion curve before you build the feature.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Infrastructure
title: API first. Browser last.
quote: The open web has been so hardened against bots. There are all these bot-identifying mechanisms, all these hard walls. I just think the web is hostile to agents right now. And we're going to have to rethink what is the interface of the web to be more agent-friendly.
bridgeText: Claire's hierarchy for any agent task: API → browser → find the problem behind the problem. Design agent integrations around stable API surfaces, not scraping. The DoorDash reframe she offers is the right PM instinct: if the agent can't order lunch, maybe it reminds you at 10:30 that you actually like eating at home. When a capability is blocked by the environment, ask whether you're solving the right problem or just the most obvious one.
actionText: For every flaky agent integration in your product or personal stack, ask: is there an API for this? If yes, switch. If no, ask what problem the user actually has — and whether there's a framing of that problem that doesn't require browser use at all.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Delegation
title: Let your agent manage you.
quote: I have my agent assign me Linear tickets for things that I need to do — not that it needs to do. Then that's in my project management system and we all agree on due dates. So let your agent project-manage your tasks as well.
bridgeText: Most people think delegation ends at 'have the agent do it.' Claire's insight is that for tasks requiring human action (make the call, sign the form, make the decision), a text reminder you'll ignore is not delegation. A ticket in your actual workflow with a real due date is delegation. The direction of project management flips: you're not managing the agent, the agent is managing you. That's the unlock.
actionText: Pick one recurring human-action task your agent currently just reminds you about via message. Have it create a task in your actual PM system (Notion, Linear, wherever you actually work) with a due date instead. Notice whether the completion rate changes.

noteTitle: 7 lessons Claire Vo taught me about managing agents
label: On Onboarding
title: Just ramble. Seriously.
quote: The highest bandwidth API for an LLM is just chatting to it. Do it on your phone and do it in voice notes. When that agent asks you for the first time, 'who are you, what do you need?' — click the voice thing and say: I'm Claire, I run ChatPRD, I've got this complicated life. You can just kind of ramble. And it actually makes sense of all that and gets you a really good outcome.
bridgeText: The instinct to write a perfect, structured system prompt is the wrong instinct for onboarding. High-bandwidth, messy natural language produces better results than a carefully engineered structured prompt — because it contains context the structured prompt would never think to include. For product design: your onboarding UX shouldn't force users into structured fields. The open-ended 'who are you and what do you need?' approach is worth studying closely.
actionText: The next time you set up or extend an agent, send a 2-minute voice note describing what you actually want instead of writing a system prompt. Then have the agent draft its own instructions from that. Compare the output to what you would have written yourself.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Hiring
title: The team you build is the company you build.
quote: The team you build is the company you build. If you have the right people, everything else will be easy and if you have the wrong people, everything else is gonna be difficult. If a founder shows the ability early in his or her career to assess talent ruthlessly and accurately, he or she can go very far with no other abilities whatsoever.
bridgeText: Every founder talks about people being the priority. Keith goes further: talent assessment is itself a learnable, practicable muscle — with a concrete feedback loop. Most founders hire and move on. The hack is a 30-day check: ask yourself 'would I make this same call again?' That loop is as predictive as measuring 12 months out, takes five minutes, and almost no one runs it. Keith also learned early that he was better at assessing people he already knew than strangers — so he initially built his teams by stealing talent from within PayPal. It wasn't scaling in the traditional sense; it was exploiting his existing signal advantage.
actionText: Set a 30-day calendar reminder after your next hire (or revisit your most recent one): would I make this call again, and what did I learn? Build the feedback loop before you need it.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Execution
title: You don't have a headcount problem. You have a barrel problem.
quote: The fundamental driver is that the number of people that can independently drive an initiative from beginning, from inception to success is very limited within any company. And if you hire more people without expanding the number of what I call barrels that can drive from inception to success, all you're doing is stacking people behind the same initiatives.
bridgeText: You've felt this: you doubled headcount and somehow shipped less. Keith's framework explains exactly why. A barrel is someone who can take an outcome off your plate, fire-and-forget, and come back to you proactively with blockers and root causes — with enough time for you to actually help. PayPal had 254 people and 12–17 barrels. Most great early-stage companies have two. More ammunition behind a single barrel doesn't increase throughput — it increases drag. When you're making a hire, the only question that matters: am I adding a barrel, or stacking ammunition behind one that already exists?
actionText: List your top 3–5 active initiatives and write the barrel's name next to each one. If two share a barrel — or you can't name one — you have a diagnostic, not a headcount problem.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Product
title: Stop talking to your customers.
quote: I hate talking to customers. I refuse to allow colleagues to talk to customers. Customers don't know what they want and they're very bad… especially for consumers. What I purchase, what I wear is not a conscious decision. And when you're consciously trying to answer a subconscious decision, you actually give misleading information even when you're trying.
bridgeText: This is the Teresa Torres insight applied by a VC: follow behavior, not words. Keith goes further — putting a customer in an interview context removes the real-world constraints that determine actual behavior. Nobody told Tony Xu they wanted a food delivery button. The insight was structural: 93% of US restaurants don't deliver. The exception is enterprise, where a decision-maker is making a mostly utilitarian choice and you can access them directly. Consumer and SMB: trust your insight, pressure-test it with behavioral or market data, not stated preferences.
actionText: Audit one product decision currently grounded in interview feedback. Can you replace or pressure-test it with a behavioral signal — retention, usage drop-off, signups, or structural market data? If not, what would you need to find it?

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Talent
title: Build on undiscovered talent. Always.
quote: You have to build a company on undiscovered talent. I don't think you really want to compete for the people that everybody else wants. I think about, why is this person going to get thrown into this black box kind of thing and not get processed accurately? And then that leads to, oh, perfect.
bridgeText: You can't out-bid Google or Stripe. Your edge is going earlier and identifying alpha others will miss. Keith's approach: figure out why a large company's hiring process will misread this specific person — and go get them first. This is structurally identical to finding an ugly-baby startup before consensus forms. For talent, younger candidates have less data on them, which means big-company evaluation machines can't process them accurately — that's your window. The reference question he swears by: 'Is this person capable of being a world-class [role]?' — not 'were they a good employee?'
actionText: For your next open role, before writing the JD, write down: what would cause Google or a top-tier company to pass on this person? That's your sourcing filter for where the alpha is.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Operations
title: Speed is a signal. It shows up early.
quote: There's a tempo, an operating tempo that a successful company develops that develops very early in a company's trajectory. At board meeting X, you guys identify an opportunity or problem and by the next board meeting, you've shipped solutions, addressed it, featured just constantly consistently. That speed really does compound.
bridgeText: Keith preempted Ramp's Series A in four months because they were about to ship a card in three — something that typically takes nine to twelve. Operational tempo isn't a symptom of success; it's the leading indicator. The metric he runs mentally: problem identified at check-in X → shipped response before check-in X+1. This is measurable from day one and visible to any observer paying attention. The moment your team starts resolving issues two cycles after you identify them, the drag coefficient has arrived.
actionText: Name one thing you identified as broken or important in your last team meeting. Is there a shipped response to it this week? If not, define the smallest version you can ship in 5 days and name who owns it.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Keith Rabois taught me about building a company
label: On Culture
title: Criticize in public. Psychological safety is for losing teams.
quote: When you give people feedback individually, you're optimizing for the atomic unit, not the system. The reason why to do it in public is it's more important for all the colleagues to understand that there's an issue. High performance machines don't have psychological safety. They're about winning.
bridgeText: This one is deliberately uncomfortable. When feedback stays private, the team doesn't know the problem is being addressed — which generates ambient anxiety and prevents colleagues who could help from raising their hand. Making feedback visible calibrates the whole room, not just the individual. If your culture is polite, you might be building a safe culture, not a winning one. Keith also inverts the conventional management logic on when to push: when things are going well, that's exactly when to be critical — because complacency is arriving in the same breath as success.
actionText: In your next team review or standup, make one piece of critical feedback visible to the group instead of routing it to a 1-1. Watch how the room responds — and notice whether anyone volunteers to help fix it.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On Timing
title: We're in 1997. Stop acting like it's 2010.
quote: We're in 1997. It's very exciting. Most stuff kind of doesn't work yet. Most of the stuff that people are going to do hasn't been built yet. And it's not really clear how any of it's going to work when it does work.
bridgeText: The pressure to have a fully-formed AI strategy right now is mostly noise. We're in the 'what is this?' phase — not the 'who won?' phase. That's not an excuse for inaction — it's an excuse to stop treating every AI hype cycle as if you're already behind.
actionText: Next time someone asks 'what's our AI strategy?', reframe the question internally: what problems do our users have that weren't solvable before? That's the 1997 question worth answering.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On What Work Really Is
title: The task isn't the job. Know the difference.
quote: Are you hiring them to get a 75 slide deck? Well, narrowly, Claude will make a really crappy version of that. But even if it was, that's not what you pay them for. The PowerPoint is just the task. But that's not what you hired them for.
bridgeText: This is the core PM trap with AI features. We get excited about automating the visible task when the actual value users pay for is the judgment, context, and decision behind it. If your AI feature handles the PowerPoint but users still need someone to tell them what to put in it, you've saved two hours and left the real problem untouched.
actionText: For any AI feature you're building or evaluating, ask: is the task we're automating actually the hard part — or is it the scaffolding? If it's scaffolding, the real product opportunity is upstream.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On Jobs
title: You can't see the new job because it doesn't exist yet.
quote: Every time we have a new technology, it automates away a bunch of jobs and then that automation unlocks a bunch of new jobs. You can always see the job that's going to go away. And you don't know the new job because it doesn't exist yet.
bridgeText: Your instinct that 'people will adapt' is historically correct. The FOMO isn't just emotionally unproductive — it's analytically wrong. Most enterprise users are not daily AI users yet. That gap between the tech-forward 20% and the mainstream 60% is the PM opportunity, not a threat.
actionText: Stop benchmarking yourself against 'AI-native' workers. Benchmark against your actual user. If your users are in that 60% still figuring it out, you're not behind — you're exactly on time.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On Competitive Moats
title: When everything's a commodity, distribution wins.
quote: Google is using distribution to drive Gemini. What's the difference between Gemini and Claude? If you're using this stuff all day, then you know. But like, normal person, there's no difference. Distribution of an adequate product — when the field is basically commodity — distribution and brand become a big deal.
bridgeText: In a world where foundation models are converging toward commodity pricing, the winner isn't the best model — it's the model that's already there when the user needs it. Your AI feature doesn't need to be the best. It needs to be in the workflow. Default status beats superior capability every time.
actionText: Audit where your product isn't in the user's default workflow. An AI feature buried in a settings menu is not distribution. One that shows up in the flow the user already lives in — that's the play.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On Disruption
title: You can't predict what gets disrupted.
quote: You can't look at a senior partner at a law firm and say, well, 17% of their work could be automated. This is horseshit. You can't predict which things are going to be exposed.
bridgeText: The frameworks for 'AI exposure scores' by job type are false precision. The disruption rarely comes from doing the same task cheaper. It comes from reframing what the task is. In 1997, the internet seemed irrelevant to taxi drivers. By 2010, it had restructured the entire industry.
actionText: For your product category, ask: what's the personal trainer equivalent? What does your product do that seems 'human' — but could be reframed as a workflow an AI handles asynchronously? That's where the blind spot is.

noteTitle: 6 lessons Benedict Evans taught me about AI
label: On What To Do About It
title: Dive in. FOMO won't save you. Fluency will.
quote: Don't stick your head in the sand and say, I hate all of this stuff. That gives you a great feeling of moral superiority. But that's not going to help. What helps is you diving into this completely — submerging yourself in it and coming out understanding what you can do with it.
bridgeText: The antidote to FOMO isn't avoidance — it's fluency. Benedict isn't saying 'learn to code AI.' He's saying build genuine understanding of what it can and can't do in your specific context. Discover as you use. Use as you discover. That loop is the whole strategy.
actionText: Pick one AI tool adjacent to something you already do and use it for 30 days on real work — not toy examples. The goal isn't expertise. It's developing the intuition for where it breaks down, so you stop being surprised by it in product decisions.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Being Right
title: A great boat in a dead lake bed isn't going anywhere.
quote: If I get to pick one thing that you do as CEO, I'm going to pick that you're right. So even if you don't operate the ship or the factory that well, I'd rather that you picked the right product, the right strategy than your phenomenal execution or inspiring people or managing — because being in the right body of water matters more than the right boat. And a great boat in a dead lake bed isn't going anywhere.
bridgeText: This reorders the job description. Not execute well, not inspire the team — be right about where you are. Everything else is a multiplier on a number that might be zero. The hiring corollary is the usable half: “Are they right? That's the best resume. I'll take misfits who are right.” The question isn't whether someone is senior or has shipped — it's whether they've been right about something before it was consensus, and whether you can see the receipt.
actionText: Pick the three people whose product judgment you weight most heavily. For each, write down one specific thing they were right about early, before the room agreed. If you can't name one, you're weighting seniority, not accuracy.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Instinct
title: Follow the instinct. Not the idea.
quote: We have these instincts like in our gut, these human level instincts that are pretty much always right. And then we put these ideas on top of the instincts that are usually wrong. My rule of thumb is your instincts are right 95% of the time, your ideas are wrong 75% — or at best right 25% of the time.
bridgeText: Instincts are singular — a read on how the world is moving. Ideas are plentiful — the shapes you wrap around that read. Conflating them is how founders die: they kill the instinct because the first idea failed, or defend a dead idea because the instinct still feels true. His own case was Tribe, a year ahead of Facebook, right instinct and wrong ideas every time. Two weeks before recording he killed his dot-earth project for the fourth time — four years and $25M on that version — and is already rebuilding toward the same instinct. He kills ideas; he never kills the instinct.
actionText: Write your instinct in one sentence — a claim about how the world is moving, with no product in it. Then list every idea you've attached to it. Which ones are you defending because the instinct is right, rather than because the idea is?

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Copying
title: If you're truly ambitious, burn your resume.
quote: It's almost a moral arbitrage. You became a founder, an entrepreneur because you wanted to go be an innovator. And so it can feel like a beat down that your path to innovation starts with copying other people's work. But that also makes that opportunity in some ways more available for people who have less ego involved.
bridgeText: He doesn't defend copying on ethical grounds — he reframes who you're performing for. “Define your ambition in the eyes of your consumer, not your peers.” The arbitrage exists precisely because founder ego prices most people out of it. And his Proven/Better/New definitions are stricter than the summaries suggest: Proven means on this platform, for this audience, for this experience — a game that worked in the 90s doesn't count. Better means 10 out of 10 existing users say yes, not you: “what you think is better is called New.” Sid Meier shipped to Facebook and Zynga's junior PMs called it dead on arrival in ten minutes, because he skipped Proven — so his innovation never got seen.
actionText: Re-label every roadmap item as Proven, Better, or New using his strict definitions — Better means 10 out of 10 existing users say yes, not you. Count how many things you called improvements that are actually unvalidated New bets in a costume.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Ambition
title: The more ambitious you are, the smaller you should start.
quote: If we're too ambitious at the outset and too visionary about the product we want to build, then we will probably miss product market fit — because we won't start at a small enough, humble enough place. Usually the starting point for these products is embarrassingly small.
bridgeText: At Tribe he tried to do all of social networking at once; pieces worked, the company failed. Then at 41, a multi-time successful founder, he made a poker game — “people thought I had no dignity.” His framing: ambition came down to a thousand-foot altitude, not a hundred thousand foot, and that was the key to it working. The sting for anyone with a track record: “it almost gives a new founder an advantage over a multi-time successful founder, because we have too much rope to hang ourselves. It's too easy to raise money and recruit teams against a big vision before we've gotten to product market fit.” Credibility is a liability at the idea stage.
actionText: Take the thing you're most excited to build and write the version that would embarrass you to describe out loud — one use case, one audience, thousand-foot altitude. If you can't bring yourself to write it, that reluctance is the diagnosis.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Hope
title: Kill hope before hope kills you.
quote: Hope is confidence without basis. And I think the best product makers, I like to say they're collecting winnings — they're not making bets. If you talk to Brian Chesky about his launches, he already knows that he has a hit. He's not launching it to find out if people like it.
bridgeText: He goes after the sacred acronym: stop shipping an MVP, ship a maximum launchable product. “Viable is the word we've got to kill along with hope — because viable is where hope comes from.” A product you ship to learn from is a different object than one you ship because you believe it's a hit; most teams blur them and get the worst of both. The test: “if you're asking whether or not your product is an A, it's not an A — and you're full of hope.” The power move isn't killing the B-plus, it's naming it. And the courage required is organizational: “the real founder mode is, can you have the courage to tell your team and your investors that this isn't it?”
actionText: Grade your current main bet A or B-plus, out loud, to one other person. If you found yourself arguing for the A, you've answered. Then write the one sentence you'd have to say to your team if it's a B-plus — and notice how hard it was to type.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Management
title: Micromanagement is beautiful — but not for the reason you think.
quote: All of management is just how do we get people to do the right thing when we're not in the room. The first principle is be in the room if you can be, as much as you can be, and then only delegate when you get to the point that you can't possibly be in all these rooms at the same time.
bridgeText: The intuitive defense of micromanagement is distrust. That's not his argument at all — his is about deployment. Every management technique is a lossy proxy for your presence, and you use a proxy only where you can't be. “If you were the best product maker in the company, we want you on the field.” And his “expert witness” is a diagnosis, not a job spec: the IC closest to the data and furthest from the decision, called to the stand then excused. “Those are the best people to turn into a CEO… they have all this pent-up demand to actually go and prove that they were right.” So you don't hire fully formed founders — you hire people who are right and have never been allowed to act on it. That resolves the apparent contradiction with “make everyone a CEO”: micromanage the craft, fully delegate the hill. The lie isn't that micromanagement is bad — it's that those two are the same knob.
actionText: Draw two columns: craft I should be in the room for, and hills I should hand over whole. Put every current commitment in one. Anything sitting in both is where you're causing damage — half-present, half-delegated.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Distribution
title: It's a quiet, lonely cocktail party.
quote: Today, we're all hanging out on our Claude, on our GPT, but there's no cocktail party. My Easter egg to people is, it's a quiet, lonely cocktail party — the web was before social networking. And my challenge to your listeners is figure out how to make it rowdy. Figure out how to make that cocktail party social and socially productive, and you will probably find gold there.
bridgeText: His structural read first: AI is not yet a platform — not hardware, not an interface layer third parties can build on. We're halfway to something, which means discovery is broken rather than merely hard. “It's not an ideal moment to launch consumer right now with high confidence.” The implication: “when distribution is this broken, it is even more core to your product and your strategy” — build-it-and-they-will-come is explicitly a hope strategy. His method for finding latent demand is to look for where the cocktail party already is, or where you could host one, then ask what lead people walk away with. Napster's lead was a music file, Friendster's a date, LinkedIn's a job.
actionText: Name the cocktail party your users are already at, and the lead they'd be thrilled to walk away with. If you can't name either, you have a distribution problem dressed up as a product problem.

noteTitle: 8 lessons Mark Pincus taught me about building products
label: On Generating
title: Build it wrong before you know it's right.
quote: AI is so powerful that it's dangerous — it means we can get to a viable product in much less time and money. Three months instead of three years. And that's a dangerous drug. What I thought would happen is that people would be using AI to build these incredible testing machines, failure machines. How are you testing 100 ideas a day instead of one in three months? I think AI is being used more to build one idea in three months than 100 ideas in a day.
bridgeText: The same principle he gives his kids — “how can you be generative and not consumptive” — pointed at work. But the sharp version isn't make things instead of scrolling. It's that AI collapsed the cost of being wrong and almost nobody restructured their process to exploit it; they just build their one wrong idea faster. “What can I believe today? I believe this is the wrong product. What are you going to do differently because you believe it's the wrong product?” The FarmVille story is the shape: the team wanted a $10M pre-launch ad budget while sitting on 25–30M daily users. He put locked art variants on the game board instead, tested which pulled, added early access — and got marketing direction, product direction, and $19M in pre-sold keys.
actionText: Take the thing you were going to spend a month building. Write down five cheap wrong versions that would each produce signal in a day — a fake ad, a locked button, a landing page, a manual concierge run. Ship one. You're buying information, not a product.
